edges.effect_quant: Direct floss evidence is mixed: a systematic review of 11 studies found most trials did not show a clear floss benefit on plaque or clinical gingivitis, but a supervised trial in 119 adults reduced interproximal bleeding by about 67% with flossing versus 35% with toothbrushing alone. Broader oral-hygiene meta-analysis also linked better home care with lower periodontitis risk.
edges.population: adults using daily flossing or closely related interdental cleaning as part of home oral hygiene
edges.mechanism: Daily flossing can disrupt plaque and food debris in narrow interproximal spaces that toothbrush bristles often miss. That may reduce gingival inflammation and, over time, lower the chance of plaque-driven periodontal breakdown when the technique is performed consistently and well.
edges.summary: The most careful interpretation is mildly protective with meaningful uncertainty. Flossing probably helps prevent some periodontal inflammation in people who can use it correctly, but the trial literature is weaker and more inconsistent than routine dental advice often implies.
edges.caveats: This edge should not be overclaimed: many flossing studies are short, technique-sensitive, and focus on plaque or gingivitis rather than long-term periodontitis incidence. The real benefit likely depends on dexterity, adherence, embrasure anatomy, and whether floss is the best interdental tool for a given person.
